# NBIS Stock Climbs as Nebius Hikes AI Inference Prices

October 15, 2026

thomz

nbis stock – Trending Topic in the US

Nebius Group is pressing ahead with a second round of price increases in a matter of weeks, lifting rates across its managed AI inference platform, Token Factory, only days after the AI infrastructure company raised fees for its on-demand cloud services. The move signals a deliberately aggressive pricing posture at a moment when demand for cloud capacity is outpacing available supply.

## Nebius Lifts Token Factory Rates Across Its Nvidia Lineup

Several posts published on X on Tuesday, which appear to be customer communications issued by Nebius, indicate the company has raised Token Factory prices by an average of 18.3%. No formal corporate announcement has confirmed the changes yet, so those notices currently serve as the primary evidence of the repricing.

The adjustments target the platform’s Pay-As-You-Go dedicated endpoints and become effective Oct. 1. According to screenshots circulating online, hourly costs for the most advanced Nvidia configurations are rising sharply across the portfolio.

### Hourly Rate Changes by GPU Configuration

- Nvidia H100: up 16%, moving from $4.05 per hour to $4.70
- Nvidia H200: up 19%, moving from $4.70 per hour to $5.60
- Nvidia B200: up 18%, moving from $7.40 per hour to $8.70
- Nvidia B300: up 20%, moving from $8.10 per hour to $9.70

Nebius indicated that existing contractual pricing and already scheduled reservations remain insulated from the updates, a distinction that matters considerably for enterprises running long-horizon model training or steady-state inference workloads. The company attributes the higher rates to sustained, intense demand for cutting-edge GPU capacity.

The Oct. 1 effective date lands ahead of the autumn holiday stretch, and investors planning around the fall trading calendar can check our Columbus Day market schedule for relevant session details.

...

### When do the new Token Factory prices take effect?

The changes apply to Pay-As-You-Go dedicated endpoints and begin on Oct. 1, according to the communications posted online.

results.title: Nebius quietly changed how it prices preemptible GPUs on October 8, a week after raising on-demand rates. | Devanshu Rajput
results.author: Devanshu Rajput
highlights:
# Nebius quietly changed how it prices preemptible GPUs on October 8, a week after raising on-demand rates. | Devanshu Rajput · LinkedIn · 2026-10-15T00:00:00+00:00

**Devanshu Rajput**: Growth & Marketing Intern @ ComputeStacker | Content Marketing | SEO | Market Research | Social Media | AI & Technology.

---

Nebius quietly changed how it prices preemptible GPUs on October 8, a week after raising on-demand rates.

Preemptible H100, H200, B200, B300 and RTX PRO 6000 moved from fixed rates to dynamic spot pricing. The published number is now a floor, not a price.

For the H100, that means "$2.15 per GPU-hour" became "from $0.79." The B300 went from $4.30 to a floor of $0.99.

The mechanics matter more than the floor. Nebius says spot prices move with capacity, utilisation and demand, can change as often as every 15 minutes, and can change during use. The ceiling is one cent below the on-demand rate for the same capacity.

So on an H100 the possible range is now $0.79 to $4.49 an hour, on the same chip, in the same region, depending on when you run.

That's a different planning problem from a fixed preemptible rate. You can model a fixed rate in a budget. A range this wide needs you to watch the actual price, not the rate card.

Two things worth knowing: this is the second Nebius change this month, after the October 1 on-demand increase, and the H100 is in one region only, eu-north1.

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Rental Prices Twice in 2026. Nebius Just Did It Again. — AIntOps
highlights:
AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block pricing for GPU instances roughly 15% in January 2026 and another 20% in July. Nebius raised its on-demand GPU prices again on October 1 — the second increase in three months, with some memory pricing up about 41%. Neither company frames these as one-time corrections. They read as a new baseline: the rental price of a GPU is no longer a number you can assume holds from one quarter to the next.

Published October 19, 2026 · 7 min read

## AWS: two hikes, one product line

AWS's EC2 Capacity Block pricing for ML instances moved twice this year. The first increase, reported to take effect around January 4-6, raised rates on the P5 family by roughly 15% — p5e.48xlarge went from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour, and p5en.48xlarge from $36.18 to $41.61. Asked about the change, an AWS spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics it reflects "the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter." The second increase landed July 1, roughly 20%, across the P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families — one report lists the P6-B300 now billing at $14.04 per accelerator-hour. Both changes applied specifically to Capacity Block reservations, not general on-demand EC2 pricing.

## Nebius: the same pattern, a shorter interval

Nebius notified customers on September 17 that on-demand AI cloud prices would rise again starting October 1 — its second increase in roughly three months. The headline move: H100 GPU-hour pricing went from $3.85 to $4.50, about 17%, with some memory pricing up roughly 41%. The company's own framing points to tight capacity, the same pressure AWS cited.

...

This is our reading ... not something ... directly: a price increase on a GPU rental line reads like an infrastructure cost, not an AI cost, in most reporting structures — it shows up in a cloud bill, under compute, often in a different review ... the one that tracks OpenAI or Anthropic API spend. If your AI workload runs partly on rented GPU capacity and partly on provider APIs, the two cost lines move independently and get reviewed by different people, on different schedules, even though both are the same underlying pressure: AI demand outpacing supply.

## Two increases a year is the new cadence to plan for

Neither AWS nor Nebius has signaled this is the last increase. Two rounds in a year, from two unrelated providers, each citing supply and demand rather than a one-off event, is a pattern worth budgeting for rather than treating as an anomaly to absorb once and move past.

results.title: Your GPU agent needs a price limit
highlights:
SF Compute now exposes upcoming price increases to agents. For local-AI builders, the useful hedge is a workload that can move when the rental math changes.

...

## The rental rate enters the control loop

On October 13, 2026, SF Compute’s Autoresearch added at least 24 hours of advance notice for price increases, including machine-readable notices for agents. Its October 8 H100 increase had arrived without advance warning: $3.96 became $5.04 per GPU-hour, including on running nodes. The company apologized. The dated changelog records both events.

The interesting development is the response. A rental agent can now see an upcoming increase through `rate.upcoming_increase` on node calls. That creates an opportunity to make price part of scheduling. It does not automatically enforce your budget; your own policy still has to decide what happens next.

...

The rates documentation also describes calendar discounts: an interactive node can cross into cheaper Friday or weekend minutes, with days defined on the US Pacific calendar. The calendar and upcoming rate are exposed in responses. But a running node can still be repriced when the list price changes. Read the current billing rules; a quoted launch rate is insufficient protection.

results.title: GPU Market Watch: Weekly Notes on GPU Cloud Supply, Demand and Pricing Moves | OpenTencor AI
highlights:
Each entry links to the primary source.

...

Reading list this week. The official pricing and announcement pages listed in the provider directory are the primary sources; check the ones for the providers you use. Where a provider has announced a change, it appears on its own pricing or blog page before anywhere else.

...

## Week of October 19, 2026

What moved (12–18 October). Four developments this week bear on budgets; each links to the primary source, and none of them is a price we publish.

- NVIDIA opened its Vera Rubin rack and compute-tray designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP Global Summit, 13–14 October). The designs were contributed through the MGX architecture, with Google, Meta and Microsoft named among adopters, so next-generation racks can be built by many manufacturers rather than one. For buyers this shortens the path from Rubin announcement to Rubin capacity in the big clouds, and it is the clearest signal yet that Hopper- and Blackwell-class cards will keep sliding into the value tier for inference. Source: NVIDIA blog.
- Scaleway announced a new GPU zone in Copenhagen built on NVIDIA HGX B300 (ai-PULSE, 13 October). No opening date was given. It adds a European option for Blackwell Ultra-class capacity, which matters if your data has to stay in the EU; treat it as a 2027 planning item until the zone is listed on Scaleway’s availability page. Source: Scaleway newsroom.
- CoreWeave is entering India with 240 MW of capacity at AdaniConneX’s Navi Mumbai campus (announced 6 October; first phase expected mid-2028). Nothing to budget for this year, but it continues the pattern this log has tracked since the summer: specialist providers are building where power and demand are, and the same card will increasingly carry a different price in each region. Source: CoreWeave news.
- AWS states on its EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing page that current prices are scheduled to be updated next in January 2027. Several third-party price trackers reported a revision to Capacity Block rates in early October; the official table remains the source of truth, and it still lists rates by Region. If Capacity Blocks are part of your plan, confirm the figure for your Region now and put a price review in your January calendar. Source: AWS Capacity Blocks pricing.

Budget implication. Nothing this week changes last week’s guidance: price inference one generation back, price training on spot with an interruption allowance, and keep term commitments short enough that a scheduled January repricing or a Rubin arrival cannot strand you. Add one item: if a provider has told you its next price update date, write it into the budget as a review date rather than treating the current figure as fixed.

results.title: The same H100 can cost $0.79 or $12.29 an hour. Both are list prices, in the same month. | Compute Stacker
results.author: Compute Stacker
highlights:
# The same H100 can cost $0.79 or $12.29 an hour. Both are list prices, in the same month. | Compute Stacker · LinkedIn · 2026-10-15T00:00:00+00:00

**Compute Stacker**.

---

The same H100 can cost $0.79 or $12.29 an hour. Both are list prices, in the same month.

The low end is Nebius preemptible, under its new dynamic spot pricing that started October 8. The high end is Azure's on-demand ND96isr H100 v5, at $98.32 per 8-GPU node.

Four purchase types, same chip:

- Preemptible and spot: Nebius from $0.79 (a floor, not a fixed price), CoreWeave spot at $19.71 per 8-GPU node, or $2.46 per GPU
- On-demand: $3.99 at Lambda, $4.50 at Nebius, $6.16 at CoreWeave, $12.29 at Azure
- Reserved: AWS Capacity Blocks moved to $5.970 per GPU-hour on October 7
- Committed: CoreWeave advertises up to 60% off on-demand, with no published tiers

The cheap tiers carry conditions. Preemptible capacity can be reclaimed, so it fits checkpointed work, not a production endpoint. Nebius's spot price can now change every 15 minutes, including during a run. Committed rates need a contract.

What this means in practice: before comparing two providers, make sure you're comparing the same purchase type. A spot rate against an on-demand rate is a 3x gap that tells you nothing about which provider is cheaper.

And re-check on the day you budget. Nebius changed its pricing twice in eight days.

results.title: Neocloud pricing climbs while AI inference costs fall — TechReaderDaily
results.author: M Mireille Otsuka Staff reporting
highlights:
The upward leg is not subtle. Nebius raised major GPU prices 17% to 21%, and short-duration capacity negotiations have reached $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, per Seeking Alpha's September analysis. CoreWeave signed new compute capacity contracts at higher prices in the third quarter of 2026, adding $25 billion in commitments. Set those against the Vera Rubin roadmap and you have a three-year contract written at 2026 prices for hardware that will produce tokens at a fraction of 2026 cost. That is a good trade for a seller with a backlog and a bad trade for a buyer who signed without a price-reset clause.

...

The checkpoint is the fourth-quarter 2026 earnings cycle, and specifically the pricing disclosure rather than the backlog disclosure. Watch whether CoreWeave and Nebius report average contract duration as stable or shortening, whether new commitments come with index-linked or token-linked pricing clauses, and whether any of them breaks out revenue from token-priced endpoints separately from GPU-hour reservations. If token-priced revenue starts appearing as its own line item with its own margin, the neoclouds will have answered the question. If it stays bundled into a single revenue number, the answer is that they would rather readers not do the division.

results.title: Hit · GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16 — SecondSource
highlights:
Hit · GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16 — SecondSource

# GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16

GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16

Scheduled check 2026-11-16 · settled 2026-11-12

Our earlier call, under recheck · Written on Oct 18, 2026

Background

The debate is how tight AI compute really is in autumn 2026: seller presentations show sharp rises on new short contracts, while public pay-as-you-go price indexes rose far less. If only new short contracts are rising, a GPU renter’s total revenue will not keep pace at once, and anyone estimating fleet revenue from seller presentations will overshoot. SecondSource reads the premium as concentrated in new marginal contracts with the fleet average lagging, while the opposing reading says the whole fleet is being repriced.

The call

SecondSource’s reading: GPU tightness in autumn 2026 shows up as a premium tied to contract length. Short contracts of 3 to 6 months and cancellable large orders run about $40 million to $60 million per MW (a megawatt of data-center power) per year, while five-year contracts run only about $10 million to $16 million.

CoreWeave, a cloud company that rents out GPUs, says it raised prices about 25% across its products in July. But average revenue per MW across its whole fleet will not catch up with that marginal price soon; a rough calculation from second-quarter figures puts it at about $7 million to $8 million.

Our bet: third-quarter 2026 revenue, annualized and divided by end-of-quarter active power, will still be below $10 million per MW per year.

Sources behind the call

CoreWeave, Inc.(SEC EDGAR,accession 0001769628-26-000429) “~25% price increase across SKUs in July 2026”

The receipt

Grace period of 14 days after CoreWeave’s Q3 2026 earnings press release (expected mid-November 2026). Take the quarterly revenue stated in the release times 4, divided by the end-of-quarter active power (GW) stated in the same release, to get annualized revenue per MW.

Read the full deep dive

Outcome

Hit (settled 2026-11-12)

On 2026-11-12 this call was settled: it held. The prediction: in the third quarter of 2026, CoreWeave's annualized quarterly revenue divided by end-of-quarter active power would still be below $10 million per MW per year, meaning price rises are concentrated in new short contracts while the fleet average lags. How it would be checked, agreed in advance: take the quarterly revenue in CoreWeave's third-quarter results release, multiply by 4, and divide by the end-of-quarter active power stated in the same release. Below $10 million per MW per year would count as a hit; at or above it, a miss. The release came out on 2026-11-10: third-quarter revenue of $3,661 million, more than 200 MW added, and active power of over 1.7 GW. $3,661 million times 4 divided by 1,700 MW is about $8.61 million per MW per year, below the $10 million line, so the call held. The release says "over" 1.7 GW, which would only push the ratio lower, and the basis matches the 1.5 GW reported for the second quarter, so the voiding condition was not triggered. Limit: this shows only that the fleet average stays below the line. It does not confirm that new short contracts price at $40 million to $60 million per MW; that figure still comes from seller presentations.

results.title: H100 price per hour in 2026: GPU rental prices by chip
highlights:
The median advertised on-demand price of an H100 GPU-hour was $3.93 in the week of 9 Nov 2026, across 44 providers — up 31% on the same week a year earlier ($2.99). The B200 moved +47% over the same year, to $8.10.

## Prices by chip

Median advertised on-demand price, $ per GPU-hour, week of 9 Nov 2026

A100$1.91 H100$3.93 H200$5.11 B200$8.10

Source: Compute Terminal Analysis GetDeploying (CC BY 4.0) Methodology v1.0-rc Updated 13 Nov 2026, 12:21 UTC

| GPU | Latest week | A year earlier | Change | Providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 | $1.91 | $1.70 | +13% | 38 |
| H100 | $3.93 | $2.99 | +31% | 44 |
| H200 | $5.11 | $3.50 | +46% | 34 |
| B200 | $8.10 | $5.50 | +47% | 23 |

Median of each provider's median advertised on-demand price. Chips with fewer providers move more from week to week.

## Two prices for the same hour

Published rate cards tell a different story from marketplaces. Our price board — built from the on-demand prices cloud providers publish — put the on-demand H100 hour at $4.11 on 13 Nov 2026, against a marketplace median of $3.93 in the week of 9 Nov 2026.

Neither number is “the” price. List prices show what providers ask for capacity on demand; marketplace medians show where spare capacity clears; reserved and contract prices, usually lower again, sit in agreements that are rarely published in full. For anyone valuing a neocloud, lending against GPUs or underwriting a datacentre lease, the spread between the three says how tight capacity is.
